title: Sikh painting
hookLine: from miniature painters to modern artists like Sobha Singh

lines: A PICTURE ON THE LIVING-ROOM WALL.
cards: A framed picture on the wall of a Punjabi living room. An old man with a white beard, eyes half closed, one hand raised in blessing, light gathering around his head.
Grandparents walk past it every morning, and it's easy to grow up taking it as a likeness. But that face came from an artist's devotion and imagination.
Behind that picture is a long line of painters who tried to put faith into color, from tiny miniatures to large modern canvases. Today's word is their work.

teach.b: First, the small pictures. Illustrated janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak, show him in little scenes: under a tree, on a road with Mardana and his rabab, talking with holy men.
Later, painters trained in the miniature styles of the Punjab hills worked for Sikh courts, painting rulers, Gurus and stories in fine detail with tiny brushes. Second, the modern canvas.

In more recent times, painters like Sobha Singh made large, soft-lit portraits of the Gurus. His Guru Nanak, gentle and luminous, is the kind of picture that ends up framed in homes and gurdwara halls.
Other modern artists paint the panth's history, its martyrs and Punjab's daily life, each in their own style. Third, an honest question.
Since these faces come from devotion and imagination, each one is an artist's offering. Some Sikhs treasure these pictures as a way into devotion.
Others are cautious, and ask that a painting never be bowed to or treated as the Guru, because for Sikhs the Guru today is the Guru Granth Sahib and the Word.

teach.h: NO ONE PAINTED THEM FROM LIFE.
teach.b: Both are said with care. Fourth, what no paint can hold.

The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, speaks of God as akaal moorat: in paraphrase, a form beyond time. A painting can show a Guru as an artist imagines him. It can't show the one the Guru pointed to.
Maybe that's the gift these pictures can give: they point past themselves.

how: Paintings of the Gurus and of Sikh history hang in homes, gurdwara halls and museums; Sikhs differ on how such pictures should be used, and they are not worshiped as the Guru.

games.q: you're a painter asked to paint Guru Nanak, and you have no likeness to work from. what do you do?
o: paint from devotion and imagination, and let it point past itself.
copy an old painting and call it a true likeness.
games.why: painters from the janamsakhi illustrators to Sobha Singh painted from devotion and imagination. some Sikhs treasure the pictures; others ask they never be treated as the Guru.

practice: If you can, find a Sikh painting, a janamsakhi scene, a hill miniature or a modern portrait; if not, bring to mind any painting of someone holy to anyone.

Let your eyes move slowly over the hands, the background, where the light falls, and ask what the painter chose to show and what they left out. Then let the picture point you past itself, toward whatever it was trying to honor.

wordCard.voice: Sikh painting. From janamsakhi scenes and hill miniatures to modern portraits like Sobha Singh's: faith offered in color, from devotion and imagination. Today's word.
